disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation) is characterized primarily by persistent patterns of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus, disorganization, forgetfulness, and frequent careless errors, without prominent hyperactive or impulsive behaviors. Onset is typically in childhood, but it is often unrecognized until academic, occupational, or role demands exceed the individual’s compensatory strategies, leading to clear functional impairment in adulthood. The course is usually chronic, with fluctuating impact depending on structure, support, and environmental demands. It is distinguished from anxiety, depression, and normal distractibility by its early onset, cross-situational persistence, and specific cognitive-attentional deficits rather than mood or situationally limited problems.

narrative.personality: Maria is a conscientious, hands-on problem solver who channels anxiety into meticulous work and self-improvement, yet can become paralyzed by overthinking and procrastination when decisions feel high stakes.
narrative.stressor: About two years ago, Maria’s shop transitioned to a more digital, fast-paced workflow, with complex diagnostic software, strict time-tracking, and multitasking across several vehicles at once, on top of growing expectations that she mentor apprentices and handle more customer communication. For most of her career she had coped by relying on routines, written checklists, and staying late to double-check her work, but the combination of new technology, constant interruptions, and pressure to finish jobs quickly began to overwhelm the ways she had always kept herself on track. Over the following months she noticed that juggling multiple repair orders, customer questions, and training tasks left her missing steps in jobs she’d previously done almost automatically, and she started avoiding the more complicated diagnostic cases she used to enjoy because they felt mentally exhausting after long days. As these issues began to affect her productivity metrics, lead to tension with her service manager, and spill over into forgotten home projects and community commitments, her mounting anxiety and fear of making an expensive mistake finally pushed her to seek psychiatric evaluation when her husband suggested that her struggles might be more than just “stress from work.”
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I feel like I’m constantly getting pulled off track at the shop and can’t seem to stay focused on one job long enough to finish it properly.”

narrative.personality: Denise is energetic, warm, and highly people-oriented, thriving on structure and teamwork while enthusiastically throwing herself into social and creative activities in her community.
narrative.stressor: Roughly two years ago, Denise was promoted from line flight attendant to a cabin crew coordinator role, which added responsibility for scheduling, paperwork, regulatory documentation, and coordinating multiple crews across varying routes, all while she and her spouse were adjusting to their last child leaving home. In the more structured cabin environment she had always relied on checklists and routines to stay on top of her duties, but the promotion required planning ahead, tracking numerous small administrative tasks, and switching between digital platforms and communications throughout the day, which exposed long-standing difficulties she’d previously been able to mask. Over time she found herself constantly shuffling between partially completed reports, misplacing notes, and feeling mentally drained by trying to keep track of who needed what and when, leading to late submissions and subtle but increasing friction with supervisors who had expected her usual reliability. When similar patterns started showing up at home—half-finished church projects, forgotten commitments for potlucks, and mounting frustration from her spouse about her scattered follow-through—she became worried that something more fundamental than “adjusting to a new role” was going on and decided to consult a psychiatrist at the urging of a colleague who had been diagnosed with adult ADHD.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since I took this coordinator role, I just can’t seem to keep all the tasks straight or get things organized the way I need to.”

narrative.personality: Keisy is a detail-focused and conscientious planner who enjoys structure and self-improvement, yet tends to overcommit to projects and become absorbed in her interests to the point of losing track of time and routine obligations.
narrative.stressor: Nearly two years ago, Keisy’s manufacturing plant expanded production and tightened quality benchmarks, which meant more simultaneous inspection lines, increased documentation requirements, and frequent protocol updates she was expected to learn and then teach to newer staff. In the past she had managed her tendency to get absorbed in conversations or hobbies by using rigid personal routines, but the accelerating pace of changes at work and the need to constantly shift attention between stations, emails, and training duties strained those coping strategies. Over the ensuing months, she noticed that informal mentoring sessions and discussions on the floor would run long, leaving her scrambling to complete logs and reports, and that after work she often lost large chunks of time tinkering with new recipes or side projects she had optimistically scheduled for the same weekend. As her supervisor began pointing out recurring delays in documentation and she herself grew frustrated with how her time seemed to slip away from her, particularly when she was talking with colleagues or friends, she sought psychiatric help hoping to understand why managing her focus and follow-through felt so much harder despite her efforts to stay organized.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Once I get talking with people, I go on and on and then I realize I’ve lost track of time and what I was supposed to be doing.”
